scripts.opening:opening:
[measured] Famous names of Prairie Avenue.

[short pause] A summer dusk on Prairie Avenue, 1904. The lamplighters have been round, the carriages are coming home from the Loop, and behind these walls sit some of the richest families in America. [short pause] People call the street Millionaire's Row: at one point 'sixteen of the 60 members of the Commercial Club of Chicago lived on Prairie Avenue'.

[short pause] Six houses on foot, 1729 to 2115 Prairie, north to south: the man who put America to sleep on trains, a farm-machine maker in a granite fortress, the piano king, the merchant prince and his son, and the meatpacker who used everything but the squeal. [short pause] Every one of these fortunes was made in Chicago in a single lifetime.

[short pause] Start at the corner of Eighteenth Street, with the biggest house on the block.
scripts.stop:pullman: [measured] 1729 Prairie, the Pullman house, built 1870 to 1876: inside, a theatre of about two hundred seats, a pipe organ and a bowling alley, and later a palm room and a great conservatory. [short pause] George M. Pullman got rich young by lifting Chicago out of its mud, jacking up whole buildings 'on average six feet without causing them any damage'. [short pause] Then he built sleeping cars, and when Lincoln's body rode home to Springfield in one, 'hundreds of thousands of people lined the route in homage'. [short pause] Pullman died in 1897, hated by the strikers of his company town, and his widow still keeps this house, which will be razed in 1922. He also hated one thing on this street. [short pause] It is right behind you.
scripts.stop:glessner: [measured] 1800 Prairie, John J. Glessner's house. [short pause] Pullman complained, 'I do not know what I have ever done to have that thing staring me in the face every time I go out of my door'. [short pause] Glessner made his money in farm machinery for the prairie farms, and two years ago his firm merged into the giant International Harvester, with him as vice president. [short pause] His architect, Henry Hobson Richardson, died weeks before building began in 1886; the family moved in on 1 December 1887 and are still here. [short pause] Sixty years from now the house will nearly be torn down, and saved in 1966 'for just $35,000'. [short pause] Across the avenue, listen for pianos.
scripts.stop:kimball: [measured] 1801 Prairie, the Kimball house of 1890, a French chateau by Solon S. Beman with a very steep slate roof and a round tower on Eighteenth Street. [short pause] William W. Kimball came to Chicago in 1857, 'beginning with only four pianos', and by 1881 his factory was 'churning out around 100 pianos and organs every week'. [short pause] This is his last summer: he 'died at his home in Chicago on December 16, 1904'. [short pause] Now walk a block south to the richest man in the city.
scripts.stop:field: [measured] 1905 Prairie, Marshall Field's house, designed by Richard Morris Hunt of New York. [short pause] Field came from Massachusetts and became 'the wealthiest and most powerful businessman in Chicago', worth $125 million by 1905. His store's rule was 'Give the lady what she wants', and the ladies made him rich. [short pause] He and George Pullman both bought land on this street, and the rest of Chicago's rich followed them here. His house will stand until 1955, when it is razed. [short pause] Next year his world will fall apart, and it starts two doors south.
scripts.stop:field-jr: [measured] 1919 Prairie, Marshall Field Jr.'s house. [short pause] He bought it in 1890 and kept growing it; in 1902 D. H. Burnham and Company built a huge addition, two years old tonight. Upstairs live his children, among them Marshall Field III, ten years old. [short pause] In November 1905 the father will be shot in this house, and within two months the grandfather will be dead too, of pneumonia caught on a New Year's golf course. The boy will grow up in England. [short pause] For now, the lights are on. [short pause] One more house, at the far end of the walk.
scripts.stop:armour: [measured] 2115 Prairie, the Kelley-Armour house, built in 1871 and home to the Armour family for nearly fifty years. [short pause] Philip D. Armour skipped the gold-rush shovels and 'started a business employing out-of-work miners to construct sluices'. [short pause] Back in Chicago he built Armour & Co., 'the world's largest food processing and chemical manufacturing enterprise', boasting that he used 'everything but the squeal'. In 1893 he gave a million dollars to found the Armour Institute of Technology. [short pause] He died in 1901; his widow still lives here, and she will outlast nearly everyone on the street. [short pause] The house itself is razed in 1937.
scripts.ending:finish:
[measured] End of the walk at 2115 Prairie. Mrs. Armour stayed: the district marker says she was among the last residents of the street, dying here in 1927. Most of the others had already gone. [short pause] After Bertha Palmer built her castle on Lake Shore Drive, 'the elite residents began to move north', and one by one these houses became boarding houses, warehouses and parking lots.

[short pause] A few survived. Glessner's fortress is still standing, and so is Kimball's chateau. [short pause] Come back after dark some night, when the street tells its ghost stories.
